anchors.text: Figure 1. Patient selection flowchart involvement in the study. CSA, critical shoulder angle; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging.
Figure 2. Repair configuration after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair with a double-row (suture bridge) technique.

Figure 3. The critical shoulder angle (CSA) is formed by a line connecting the inferior with the superior border of the glenoid fossa and another line connecting the inferior border of the glenoid with the most inferolateral point of the acromion. The acromial index (AI) is the distance from the glenoid plane to the lateral border of the acromion (GA) divided by the distance from the glenoid plane to the most lateral aspect of the humeral head (GH).
Figure 4. The signal intensity was calculated at the (1) rotator cuff tendon site as well as (2) the background site approximately 2 cm anterior to the shoulder.
Figure 5. The retear pattern on postoperative oblique coronal magnetic resonance imaging in shoulders with recurrent tear (white arrow) after rotator cuff repair.
Figure 6. Correlation between the critical shoulder angle (CSA) and the tendon signal/noise quotient (SNQ) value. There was a significant positive association between the CSA and tendon SNQ value.
Figure 7. Correlation between the acromial index (AI) and the tendon signal/noise quotient (SNQ) value. There was a significant positive association between the CSA and tendon SNQ value.

Figure 8. A 43-year-old woman with a large critical shoulder angle (CSA) had a tendon retear: (A) radiograph and (B) magnetic resonance image. White arrow indicates retear tendon. (See Figure 3 for angle definitions.)

Figure 9. Comparison of tendon signal/noise quotient (SNQ) between the large critical shoulder angle (CSA) group and the control group. ##Significant difference between groups, P = .003. Values are presented as mean ± SD.

(G) Zeta potential and particle size of CZPDC at different pH values. (H) The pore size distribution of CZPDC, illustrated as a pie chart of pore volume contributions from micropores, mesopores, and macropores.

FIGURE 2 | Valence distribution and coordination environment of CZPDC. (A) Ce, (B) Zr, (C) O fine spectra in x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy of CZPDC. (D) The K-edges XANES of Zr element in Zr-foil, ZrO₂ and CZPDC, the illustration showed the peak in front of the edge. (E) Fourier transform EXAFS spectra of Zr-foil, ZrO₂ and CZPDC. (F) WT for the K³-weighted EXAFS signals of Zr in CZPDC. (G) The K-edges XANES of Ce element in CeO₂ and CZPDC. (H) Fourier transform-EXAFS spectra of CeO₂ and CZPDC. (I) WT for the K³-weighted EXAFS signals of Ce in CZPDC.

FIGURE 3 | The CZPDC-catalyzed hydrolysis effect and mechanism verification of glycoside small molecules. (A) Michaelis–Menten curve and (B) Lineweaver–Burk plot for PNPG hydrolysis, 250 µg/mL CZPDC, 40°C, pH 8.0. (C) Michaelis–Menten curve and (D) Lineweaver–Burk plot for 4-MUG hydrolysis, 250 µg/mL CZPDC, 40°C, pH 8.0. (E) Mass spectra of PNPG hydrolysis products in H₂O and H₂¹⁸O. (F) Mass spectra of PNPG hydrolysis products in H₂O and H₂¹⁸O. (G) The hydrolysis reaction equations of PNPG and 4-MUG. (H) BET curves of CZPDC before and after hydrolysis of PNPG. (I) Fluorescence spectrum of coumarin mixed with MOF to verify whether free radicals are generated during the reaction process. (J) CZPDC-catalyzed hydrolysis of PNPG and 4-MUG in air and vacuum, respectively. (K) CZPDC catalyzed 4-MUG in 10% (v/v) isopropanol/water. The data are represented as mean ± SD, with different letters indicating differences of p < 0.05.

FIGURE 4 | Catalytic mechanism of CZPDC. The hydrolysis pathway of (A) PNPG and (B) 4-MUG catalyzed by CZPDC. Transition state and intermediate free energy changes during CZPDC-catalyzed hydrolysis of (C) PNPG and (D) 4-MUG. The illustration shows the corresponding state structure calculated by DFT.

FIGURE 5 | The anti-biofilm ability of CZPDC. (A) and (B) illustrated the inhibitory effect and the ability to remove mature biofilms of different concentrations of CZPDC on the formation of E.coli biofilm. The data are represented as mean ± SD, with different letters indicating differences of $p < 0.05$. (D) and (E) illustrated the inhibitory effect and the ability to remove mature biofilms of S. aureus. biofilm. The data are represented as mean ± SD, with different letters indicating differences of $p < 0.05$. (C) and (F) respectively described the biofilm growth of E. coli and S. aureus at 6, 12, and 24 h, and the SEM images after adding 250 μg/mL CZPDC at 6, 12, and 18 h. (G) and (H) showed the CLSM images and fluorescence intensity statistics of biofilm formed by E. coli and S. aureus without/after 12 h of CZPDC treatment. The fluorescence intensity was obtained by measuring the green fluorescence intensity of 100 μm × 100 μm in 5 different locations with ImageJ, expressed as mean ± SD.

FIGURE 6 | Anti-bacterial activity of CZPDC. (A) and (B) demonstrate the bactericidal ability of CZPDC at different concentrations against E. coli and S. aureus. The data are represented as mean ± SD, with different letters indicating differences of $p < 0.05$. The illustration shows photos of culture media containing bacteria treated with different concentrations of CZPDC. (C) and (D) show the ssDNA and protein concentration obtained when E. coli and S. aureus were treated with different concentrations of CZPDC. The data are represented as mean ± SD, with different letters indicating differences of $p < 0.05$. (E) and (G) show CLSM images of E. coli and S. aureus stained with Calcein-AM and PI, when treated with different concentrations of CZPDC for 2 h. (F) and (H) show the fluorescence intensity statistics of bacteria by E. coli and S. aureus without/after CZPDC treatment. The fluorescence intensity was obtained by measuring the green fluorescence intensity of 80 μm × 100 μm in 5 different locations with ImageJ, expressed as mean + SD.

FIGURE 7 | Biological toxicity of CZPDC. (A) Stained images of different visceral slices in mice. Administer 200 μL of 50 μg/mL, 200 μg/mL, and 500 μg/mL CZPDC by gavage to mice (Control PBS). All mice were euthanized and dissected for staining analysis after 10 days. Cell survival rates of (B) L929, (C) A549, and (F) HepG2 after treatment with different concentrations of CZPDC. The data are represented as mean ± SD, with different letters indicating differences of p < 0.05. (D) Hemolysis test of CZPDC on rabbit blood, (1) 50 μg/mL, (2) 100 μg/mL, (3) 200 μg/mL, (4) 500 μg/mL, (5) 1000 μg/mL, (6) negative control, (7) positive control. (E) ICP-OES results of metal element content in mouse feces at different cultivation times.

anchors.text: Figure 1. Force-electric conversion hydrogel microspheres (Piezo@CR MPs) for cartilage injury treatments. A) Preparation scheme of the Piezo@CR MPs. B) Schematic diagram of Piezo@CR MPs induce directional migration of stem cells and promote chondrogenic differentiation. Electrical stimulation generated by intra-articularly injected Piezo@CR MPs under ultrasonic activation disrupts electrostatic interactions with peptides, releasing them to induce directed migration of stem cells toward the microspheres. Sustained weak electrical stimulation was then provided at the cellular level to drive calcium inward flow by opening voltage-gated ion channels, sustained were electrical stimulation was then provided at the cellular level, driving calcium inward flow by opening voltage-gated ion channels to activate calmodulin and calmodulin, followed by activation of p38 MAPK to promote chondrogenic differentiation of stem cells to repair cartilage damage.

Figure 2. Preparation and characterization of injectable piezoelectric hydrogel microspheres. A) Representative TEM and corresponding selected area electron diffraction images of BT nanoparticles (inset image). B) Representative high resolution TEM image of BT nanoparticles. Piezo-responsive phase curve C) and amplitude curve D) of BT nanoparticles. E) Representative SEM images of piezoelectric hydrogel microspheres modified with pDA. F) The loading efficiency of stem cell recruitment peptides (CR) in hydrogel microspheres. G) Representative SEM image and the corresponding elemental mapping images of Piezo@CR MPs. H) A schematic diagram of the electrical output detection device. I) Output open-circuit voltage waveforms of piezoelectric hydrogel microspheres in deionised water under US activation. J) Output short-circuit current waveforms of piezoelectric hydrogel microspheres in deionized water under US activation. K) Release curves of stem cell-recruiting peptide from the HM@CR MPs (Nonpiezo sample) and the 2% Piezo@CR MPs (Piezo sample) under US activation. The red colored area represents times at which US was applied.

Figure 3. Injectable Piezo@CR MPs recruit cells. A) Schematic of the peptide release from microspheres to recruit cells triggered by US. The charge redistribution within the BT nanoparticles was activated by US, which disrupted the electrostatic adsorption between the peptide and the microspheres. Simultaneously, the vibration generated by US promoted the release of peptide. B) Representative images of live/dead staining of BMSCs after 2D co-culture with Piezo@CR MPs. C) Representative images of SEM (i) and live/dead staining (ii) of BMSCs after 3D co-culture with Piezo@CR MPs in low-adhesion well plates. The green area represents BMSCs. D) Representative images of crystal violet staining of migrated BMSCs from the upper chamber of a Transwell plate after co-culture with Piezo@CR MPs for 48 h. E) Representative images of live/dead staining of BMSCs in the scratched area after co-culture with Piezo@CR MPs for 5 days. F) Counts of migrated BMSCs after 2D co-culture with Piezo@CR MPs. G) Areas of adherent BMSCs covering microspheres after 3D co-culture with Piezo@CR MPs in low-adhesion well plates. H) Counts of migrated BMSCs from the upper chamber after co-culture with Piezo@CR MPs for 48 h. I) Healing rate of scratches after co-culture with Piezo@CR MPs for 5 days. (In all datasets, n = 3 independent samples, the data are expressed as mean ± SD. ns = not significant, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, and ***p < 0.001.)

Figure 4. Injectable Piezo@CR MPs promote chondrogenic differentiation of BMSCs. A) Schematic of electrical stimulation generated from Piezo@CR MPs for promoting BMSCs chondrogenic differentiation activated by US. Charges were redistributed within the BT nanoparticles inside the microspheres when activated by US, the integrated electrical stimulation enhanced the influx of calcium ions into the cells, which promoted the differentiation of stem cells toward cartilage. B) Relative expression of the cartilage genes ACAN, COL2A1 and SOX-9 was examined by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). C) Protein level of ACAN, COL2A1 and SOX-9 was examined by protein blotting (WB). D) Proteins of ACAN, COL2A1 and SOX-9 (green), cytoskeleton (red) and nucleus (blue) of BMSCs on different hydrogel microspheres were visualized by immunofluorescence (IF) staining. E) Glycosaminoglycans (GAG) in BMSCs after co-culture with different hydrogel microspheres for 14 days was examined by Alcian blue staining. F) GAG in BMSCs pellets after co-culture with different hydrogel microspheres for 14 days was examined by Alcian blue staining. G) Protein of COL2A1 (green) of BMSCs pellets after co-culture with different hydrogel microspheres for 14 days was visualized by IF staining. (In all datasets, n = 3 independent samples, the data are expressed as mean ± SD. ns = not significant, ***p < 0.001.)

Figure 5. Therapeutic effects of Piezo@CR MPs enhance cartilage regeneration in a rabbit osteochondral defect model. A) Study design of Piezo@CR MPs treatment for osteochondral defects in rabbits. B) Representative gross and micro-CT reconstructed images of defect only, non-piezoelectric and piezoelectric (Piezo@CR) hydrogel microsphere groups with US activation (1 month). Red circles represent defective areas. C) Representative gross and micro-CT reconstructed images of defect only, non-piezoelectric and piezoelectric (Piezo@CR) hydrogel microsphere groups with US activation (2 month). D) Representative images of H&E, Safranin O/Fast Green and IHC for COL2A1 staining on rabbit femur sections of defect-only, nonpiezo and piezo (Piezo@CR) hydrogel microsphere groups with US activation (1 month). E) Representative images of H&E, Safranin O/Fast Green and IHC for COL2A1 staining on rabbit femur sections of defect only, nonpiezo and piezo (Piezo@CR) hydrogel microsphere groups with US activation (2 month). F) International Cartilage Repair Society (ICRS) macroscopic cartilage assessment scores of rabbit femurs after 1,2 months without (or with) US activation. G) Subchondral bone volume of rabbit femurs after 1,2 months without (or with) US stimulation based on micro-CT reconstruction. anchors.text: Fig. 1 a) Bigliani et al $ ^{5} $ classified the acromion into three types: type I represents a flat, type II a curved and type III a hooked acromion. b) Supraspinatus outlet view demonstrating the assessment of the shape of the acromion according to Park et al. $ ^{6} $ Three points are drawn on the undersurface of the acromion: the most anterior point (A), the most posterior point (B) and the point (C) which is equidistant from the two other points. Point (O) represents the centre of the humeral head. If point C lies on the line connecting point A to B, then the acromion is a type I. If the distances OA and OC are equal, then the acromion is a type II. If the distance OA is shorter than the distance OC, then it is a type III acromion. c) Supraspinatus outlet view showing the measurement of the acromial slope according to Aoki et al. This is determined between a line drawn on the undersurface of the acromion and another line connecting the postero-inferior border of the acromion with the inferior border of the coracoid process and is called the  $ \alpha $-angle.
Fig. 2 The lateral acromion angle is determined on coronal MR arthrograms and represents the angle enclosed between the glenoid plane and the undersurface of the acromion.

Fig. 3 a) True AP radiographs with the humerus in neutral rotation are used to determine the lateral extension or the acromion. Ine distance from the glenoid plane to the lateral border of the acromion (GA) is divided by the distance from the glenoid plane to the lateral aspect of the humeral head (GH) and called the acromion index. A high acromion index represents an acromion that projects far laterally and covers the biggest portion of the humeral head. b) The critical shoulder angle is measured on true AP radiographs and corresponds to the angle formed between the glenoid plane and a line connecting the inferior glenoid rim with the lateral aspect of the acromion.

Fig. 4 Drawing demonstrating the correlation between AI and critical shoulder angle. Both parameters depend on the inclination of the glenoid and the lateral extension of the acromion. The AI and the critical shoulder angle decrease when the glenoid is oriented downwards and they increase when the glenoid is faced upwards.

Fig. 5 The acromio-humeral distance and the orientation of the force vectors of the deltoid and supraspinatus depend on the inclination of the glenoid. Upward inclination decreases the subacromial space, decreases the ascending force component of the deltoid and increases the ascending force component of the supraspinatus.

Fig. 6 The lateral deltoid winds around the humeral head and therefore exerts not only an ascending force on the humeral shaft but also a compressive force on the humeral head. The resultant deltoid force (red vector) corresponds to the sum of these forces and is in line with the deltoid muscle fibres at their origin on the acromion. A large acromion is therefore associated with a high ascending force component and a short acromion with a high compressive force component.

Fig. 7 Photographs of a cadaver shoulder specimen. The cuff was preloaded with use of thin sutures. Changing the position of the arm from adduction (a) to abduction and internal rotation (b) deformed the tendons.

Fig. 8 Photographs showing the supraspinatus tendon stumps of three cadaver shoulders, in adduction (images on the left side) and in abduction (images on the right side). One specimen had a normal tendon (a), one specimen showed degenerative changes (b) and one specimen had a cleavage lesion (c). The tendons were cut in adduction, about 1.5 cm from their insertion on the greater tuberosity and perpendicular to the tendon surface, and they were preloaded with thin sutures on the bursal and articular side. In abduction, the cutting surface of the normal tendon was no longer perpendicular to the tendon surface, indicating that the superior fibrils glided over the inferior fibrils. In the other two specimens with degenerative changes the cutting surface did not change its orientation during abduction, indicating that the tendon fibrils could not glide against each other.

FIG. 2. Commonly used mechanical and osmotic loading explant experiments; (a) Confined compression with a rigid confining chamber and a rigid, permeable-porous loading platen (top); (b) Unconfined compression with two frictionless or frictional impermeable loading platens; (c) Hydrostatic pressure loading by pressurizing the bath solution; (d) Osmotic pressure loading using solutions with known osmotic pressure (e.g., polyethylene glycol solution of known concentration); (e) The 'equivalent' mechanical loading to the osmotic pressure loading in (d)—the mechanical load must be applied isotropically onto the explant with the applied load equal to the osmotic pressure applied in (d), and exactly normal to the surface.

FIG. 3. Illustration of the MEC events experienced by chondrocytes and the interaction between ECM and chondrocytes;  $ \Delta\pi^* $ is the osmotic pressure jump and  $ \Delta\psi $ is the electrical potential jump across the cell membrane, respectively.
FIG. 4. Illustration of ECM pre-stress and osmotic pressure inside articular cartilage that is subjected to applied loading at the articular surface.

FIG. 5. Illustration of the one-dimensional permeation experiment;  $ (c_u^* $ and  $ c_d^*) $ are the NaCl concentrations upstream and downstream respectively; similarly  $ (p_u^* $ and  $ p_d^*) $ and  $ (\psi_u^* $ and  $ \psi_d^*) $ are the fluid pressures and electrical potentials respectively. The difference ( $ \Delta $) of each quantity (i.e., the motive force) will cause fluid flow, ion transport and streaming potentials.

FIG. 6. Effect of cartilage fixed charge density (FCD) on the electrical potential difference between the external upstream and downstream solutions in a one-dimensional permeation experiment. The applied hydrostatic pressure difference is 0.05 MPa; RT/Fc is approximately 25.7 mV.

FIG. 7. Distributions of flow-induced compaction (a) and FCD (b) within the tissue under various applied pressure differences ( $ \Delta p^{*} $) in a one-dimensional permeation experiment. Before compression, the initial FCD ( $ c^{F}_{0} $) is 0.2 mEq/ml.

FIG. 8. Schematic representation of fluid exudation and redistribution within cartilage during a rate-controlled, confined compression, stress-relaxation experiment (lower left). The horizontal bars in the upper figures indicate the distribution of strain in the tissue over the duration of the experiment. The lower graph (lower right) shows the stress response during the compression phase (O,A,B) and the relaxation phase (B,C,D,E).

FIG. 9. The total stress and fluid pressure in a confined compression, stress-relaxation experiment. At the impermeable surfaces, nearly the entire total stress is supported by the fluid pressure. In contrast, at the permeable surface, only a small fraction of the total stress is supported by the fluid, with the remainder borne by the solid matrix.

FIG. 10. Effect of initial fixed charge density (FCD) on peak stress ( $ p_{B} $) in a confined compression, stress-relaxation experiment. This result illustrates another beneficial contribution of FCD to the biomechanical function of articular cartilage.

FIG. 11. Schematic representation of deformation and fluid flow within cartilage during a load-controlled (creep), unconfined compression experiment (left top). The bars within the right boxes indicate the distribution of radial strain in the tissue, and the arrows indicate the distribution and magnitude of flow rate. Since the tissue is in tension in the radial direction, the vertical grid indicates the radial distribution of tensile strain. The lower left graph shows the time history of the radial displacement at the edge of the specimen (r=a).

The inset shows a cut-away view of one cartilage holder, with a thermistor inserted through the screw and containing a cartilage disk, and the agarose bridge insert. The cylindrical electrode and the tubing connector ends were threaded and screwed into the long center tube. For experiments with 12 stimulated and 12 control disks, the stimulation chamber shown here was connected to an identical chamber via tubing (Tygon; Norton, Akron, OH, U.S.A.) fitted to the tubing connector. A second pair of connected stimulation chambers were used for the controls. For experiments with six stimulated and six control disks, a second electrode replaced the tubing connector. Again, a second stimulation chamber was used for the controls.

Total radiolabel incorporation, normalized to cartilage wet weight for experimental/control disks as a function of current density and frequency (t*, w*, p < 0.05; t+, w+, p < 0.02, with the t test and Wilcoxon test, respectively). FIG. 4. The variation in total radiolabel incorporation ratios between disks from the same core position is less than that between disks from different cores. Experimental/control ratios (counts per minute [cpm]/wet weight) plotted for averages of two pairs of matched disks from the same core position (1rm = position 1, right medial; 2lm = position 2 left medial; and 5lm = position 5, left medial surface) are shown next to the mean for all six disks stimulated with 24 mA/cm² at 100 Hz (see Fig. 3).

FIG. 5. Gel fluorographs. (A) Cartilage disks incubated and labeled at 37 or 43°C for 6 hours. The heat-induced proteins are clearly apparent at 43°C. (B) Cartilage disks labeled in a 6-hour electrical stimulation experiment at 2 mA/cm² at 10 Hz. No agarose bridges were used to separate the electrodes from the cartilage disks. E1-E3 correspond to electrically stimulated disks. E1 corresponds to a disk located at one end of the chamber, adjacent to the electrode; E3, to a disk located in one middle position in the chamber; and E2, to a disk between the two. The 70 kDa stress protein (SP70) is apparent in lanes E1 and E2. (C) E1-E3 correspond to disks incubated in medium taken from the chamber adjacent to each cartilage holder position after the same electrical experiment. The media was taken from between the electrode and the first disk (E1), between the first and second disk (E2), and from the middle of the chamber (E3). SP70 is apparent in lane E1. (D) Disks labeled during a 12-hour electrical stimulation experiment in which agarose bridges were used (as in all experiments reported here). No stress proteins are seen in any lane.

anchors.text: Fig. 1: Flow chart of the study design. AKI: acute kidney injury; CKD: chronic kidney disease; ML: machine learning; PICU: pediatric intensive care unit; RF: random forest; SHAP: SHapley Additive explanation.

Fig. 2: Performance of ML models to predict AKI. (A) ROC curves of the top five best-performing ML models. (B) AUCs of the top five best-performing ML models with varied numbers of features. (C) AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score of the RF model with varied numbers of features. AdaBoost: adaptive boosting; AKI: acute kidney injury; AUC: area under the ROC curve; GBM: gradient boosting machine; LightGBM: light gradient boosting machine; ML: machine learning; RF: random forest; ROC: receiver-operating-characteristic; XGboost: eXtreme gradient boosting.

Fig. 3: Global model explanation by the SHAP method. (A) SHAP summary bar plot. (B) SHAP summary dot plot. The probability of AKI development increases with the SHAP value of a feature. A dot is made for SHAP value in the model for each single patient, so each patient has one dot on the line for each feature. The colors of the dots demonstrate the actual values of the features for each patient, as red means a higher feature value and blue means a lower feature value. The dots are stacked vertically to show density. (C) SHAP dependence plot. Each dependence plot shows how a single feature affects the output of the prediction model, and each dot represents a single patient. For example, both a low actual value  $ \leq $57.7 mmHg or a high actual value  $ \geq $96.3 mmHg of MAP_min push the decision towards the "AKI" class. SHAP values are represented by the y-axis, and actual values are represented by the x-axis. The SHAP values for specific features exceeding zero push the decision towards the "AKI" class. AKI: acute kidney injury; APTT: activated partial thromboplastin time; BUN: blood urea nitrogen; eGFR: estimated glomerular filtration rate; MAP: mean arterial pressure; PRISM III: pediatric risk of mortality III; SHAP: SHapley Additive explanation; TBil: total bilirubin; UO: urine output.

Fig. 4: Local model explanation by the SHAP method. (A–F) Waterfall plot and evolution of risks contributed by each feature for individual child at low (A–C) or high (D–F) risk of developing AKI: A and D represented the individual child towards the "AKI" class, and B and E represented the individual child towards the "non-AKI" class. In C and F, all the input features were standardized to zero-mean and unit-variance. (G) Force plot for the internal validation set. Each patient was represented by the x-axis, while the features' contributions were represented by the y-axis: an increased red part for each individual patient represented a greater probability towards the decision of "AKI". AKI: acute kidney injury; APTT: activated partial thromboplastin time; BUN: blood urea nitrogen; eGFR: estimated glomerular filtration rate; MAP: mean arterial pressure; PRISM III: pediatric risk of mortality III; SHAP: SHapley Additive explanation; TBil: total bilirubin; UO: urine output.

Fig. 5: Convenient application for clinical utility. The convenient application of the final RF model with 8 features is available for AKI prediction. When entering actual values of the 8 features, this application automatically displays the probability of 85.31%. Meanwhile, the force plot for individual child indicates the features that contribute to the decision of "AKI": the blue features on the right are the features pushing the prediction towards the "non-AKI" class, while the red features on the left are pushing the prediction towards the "AKI" class. AKI: acute kidney injury; RF: random forest.

Fig. 6: Comparison of the incidence rate and clinical variables according to the final model and KDIGO criteria. (A) Flow chart describing 1823 children subgrouped according to the final model and KDIGO criteria. AKI was defined based on serum creatinine and urine output in accordance with the KDIGO criteria. Prediction model (-) represented children with a probability <30.8%, and prediction model (+) represented children with a probability ≥30.8% in the final model. (B) MODS (P < 0.001), Shock/DIC (P < 0.001), and PICU mortality (P < 0.001) among subgroups. (C) Heatmap of the distribution of clinical and laboratory variables. Variables with a statistical difference among four subgroups (P < 0.05) were included. Each variable was standardized to zero-mean and unit-variance. The color gradient was used to show differences in mean values, with red for higher values and blue for lower values. Max and min represented the maximum and minimum values during the first 24 h after PICU admission, respectively. *P < 0.05 vs. subgroup 1, #P < 0.05 vs. subgroup 2, &P < 0.05 vs. subgroup 3.

anchors.text: Figure 1: Patient selection flowchart for the study. Flow diagram showing the patient inclusion and exclusion criteria for the study. Patients were divided into a training set (center A: Asan Medical Center, Korea) and external test set 1 (center B: Ajou University Hospital, Korea), an external test set 2 (center A: Asan Medical Center), and an external test set 3 (center A: Asan Medical Center). HCC = hepatocellular carcinoma, RFA = radiofrequency ablation.

Figure 2: Schematic representation of the MRI-based Early Recurrence Individualized Score (MERIS) and Pathology-based Early Recurrence Individualized Score (PERIS). (A) MERIS is calculated as: (AST > 29.5 IU/L × 2) + (tumor size in cm × 1) + (nonsmooth tumor margin × 2) + (peritumoral HBP hypointensity × 3). (B) PERIS is calculated as: (AST > 29.5 IU/L × 2) + (tumor size in cm × 1) + (MVI-positive × 1) + (P53 overexpression × 2). AST = aspartate aminotransferase, HBP = hepatobiliary phase, MVI = microvascular invasion.

Figure 3: Kaplan-Meier survival curves show recurrence-free probabilities stratified by risk scores. Risk stratification used a cutoff of 5 determined by the Youden index, which shows differences in probability outcomes between the risk groups. Kaplan-Meier curves show clear separation of high- versus low-risk groups by MRI-based Early Recurrence Individualized Score (MERIS) in the (A) training set (P < .001) and (B) external test set (P < .001). Pathology-based Early Recurrence Individualized Score (PERIS) stratifies the recurrence risk in the (C) training set (P < .001). However, PERIS shows no difference in probability outcomes between the risk groups in the (D) external test set (P = .07). Shaded areas indicate 95% CIs.

Figure 4: Axial gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI scans in a 63-year-old woman with recurrent hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) at 18 months of follow-up and a high MRI-based Early Recurrence Individualized Score (score of 11) show a 4-cm hepatic mass in liver segment 3. (A) Prominent arterial-phase hyperenhancement (arrowhead) is noted with (B) enhancing capsule (arrowhead) in the portal venous phase, consistent with HCC. (C) Hepatobiliary phase image shows nonsmooth tumor margins with wedge-shaped peritumoral hypointensity (arrowhead). The preoperative serum aspartate aminotransferase level is 32 IU/L, higher than the cutoff determined by the Youden index (29.5 IU/L). Partial hepatectomy was performed, and pathologic analysis showed conventional HCC with P53 overexpression but no microvascular invasion. The patient's Pathology-based Early Recurrence Individualized Score is 8. At the 18-month follow-up, the arterial-phase gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI scan shows a new focus of arterial hyperenhancement in segment 7 (arrow in D) that was absent on the preoperative MRI scan (arrow in C). The lesion shows portal venous phase washout (arrow in E) and a corresponding hepatobiliary phase defect (arrow in F), consistent with recurrent HCC.

Figure 5: Representative axial gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI scans in a 39-year-old man with no hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) recurrence at follow-up and a low MRI-based Early Recurrence Individualized Score (score of 5) shows a 5-cm hepatic mass in liver segment 7. (A) Precontrast T1-weighted image shows a 5-cm hypointense mass (arrowhead). (B) Subtle arterial phase hyperenhancement is noted with prominent intratumoral arteries (arrowheads). (C) The mass does not show definite washout in the portal venous phase (arrowhead). (D) T2-weighted imaging shows intermediate hyperintensity (arrowhead) with (E) diffusion restriction (arrowhead). (F) Hepatobiliary phase image shows smooth margins without peritumoral hypointensity (arrowhead). The preoperative serum aspartate aminotransferase level is 19 IU/L, which is lower than the cutoff determined by Youden index (29.5 IU/L). Partial hepatectomy showed conventional HCC without microvascular invasion or P53 overexpression. The patient's Pathology-based Early Recurrence Individualized Score is 5. No recurrence has been reported to date.

The arrow indicates the direction of cell migration. The migration tracks of a few cells are shown from start (yellow dots) to end of 15 hour study period (yellow lines). Scale bar is shown.

Fig 4. MSCs migrate towards the cathode (negative electrode) under EF stimulation. All plot charts depict migration over a 15 hour period. The blue marker indicates the centre of mass (the average of the x and y coordinates), red colour indicates cell migration towards the anode, and black colour indicates cell migration towards the cathode.

Fig 5. Confocal images indicating focal adhesion complexes (FACs) (A1) and cell morphology (A2) at 15 hours of no EF, and focal adhesion complexes (B1) and cell morphology (B2) with EF exposure. FACs were stained with vinculin (red), actin with phalloidin (green), and DNA with Hoescht (blue). (C) cell orientation with EF exposure. (D) cell circularity with EF exposure (E) cell viability with EF exposure (F) cellular elongation with EF exposure occurred except for at 5 V/cm. (G) The surface area of cell attachment decreased relative to controls (no EF) over time, (H) cell processes were randomly oriented after 5 hours in controls (no EF) (i), and after 5 hours under a 0.5 V/cm EF (ii), there was a clear predilection for cathodally-directed lameltopodia after 5 hours of 1.2 V/cm EF (iii), after 5 hours of 2 V/cm EF (iv) or 3 V/cm EF (v), the extension of cellular processes towards the cathode was marked. Lameltopodia were not seen when cells were exposed to 5 V/cm for 5 hours (vi). The arrows indicate the direction of the cathode. Scale bars are shown.

Fig 6.(A) Speed of migration for Donor A cells over the various times shown. There was a significant increase in migration speed for EF exposed cells compared to control cells for 0.2 V/cm at 10 hours, 0.5 V/cm at 15 hours, 1.7 V/cm at 5 and 10 hours, 2 V/cm and 3 V/cm for all time periods shown, and 5 V/cm at 10 hours. (B) euclidean distance travelled for Donor A cells at various times shown. There was a statistically significant increase in eudlidean distance for EF exposed cells compared to control cells for 0.2 V/cm at 15 hours, 1.2 V/cm at 10 and 15 hours, and 1.7 V/cm, 2 V/cm and 3 V/cm at all time periods.

Fig 6.(A) Speed of migration for Donor A cells over the various times shown. There was a significant increase in migration speed for EF exposed cells compared to control cells for 0.2 V/cm at 10 hours, 0.5 V/cm at 15 hours, 1.7 V/cm at 5 and 10 hours, 2 V/cm and 3 V/cm for all time periods shown, and 5 V/cm at 10 hours. (B) euclidean distance travelled for Donor A cells at various times shown. There was a statistically significant increase in eudlidean distance for EF exposed cells compared to control cells for 0.2 V/cm at 15 hours, 1.2 V/cm at 10 and 15 hours, and 1.7 V/cm, 2 V/cm and 3 V/cm at all time periods.

Fig 7. Donor B cells' control and experimental populations did not show significant differences in migration speed (A), but did show differences in (B) euclidean distance (significantly lower at 0.5 V/cm for all time points, and significantly higher for 1.7 V/cm at 10 and 15 hours).
Fig 8. Donor C cells' control and experimental populations showed significant differences in (A) migration speed, and (B) euclidean distance.

Fig 9. Migration towards the cathode (as shown by the arrow) was found for 2 other donor MSC populations under EF stimulation at 5 hours (A), 10 hours (B) and 15 hours (C). The directional response in Donor C 5 V/cm group was significantly different from other donors at 5 and 15 hours, suggesting differences in tolerance of different donors to stronger EF strength.

anchors.text: Figure 1. Mechano-iontronic effect for promoting cartilage regeneration. a) MI-hydrogel implanted in an articular cartilage defect. b) Mechano-iontronic conversion in MI-hydrogel. c) Comparison between MI-hydrogel with some other tissue repairing methods. d) Schematic diagram of intracellular metabolism for cells with coupled iontronic and mechanical stimulations: the opening of Piezo1 is promoted, which is a kind of mechanically-gated ion channel protein, and then led to enhanced glutamine transport, improving the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. These changes in the metabolic microenvironment significantly enhanced the repair and reconstruction of cartilage tissue.

Figure 2. Mechano-iontronic conversion in cartilage and MI-hydrogel. a) Schematic illustration of the mechano-iontronic conversion in cartilage (left) and MI-hydrogel (right). b) Electrical signal test equipment of the mechano-iontronic conversion in cartilage and MI-hydrogel. c) Measured voltage signals when applying indentation at different points of cartilage. f) Measured electrical signals of different MI-hydrogels. COMSOL simulation of mechano-iontronic conversion, d,g) pore pressure of cartilage (d) and MI-hydrogel (g); e,h) potential curves of cartilage (e) and MI-hydrogel (h). i) Equivalent piezoelectric coefficient of MI-hydrogel. j) Cyclic stability of MI-hydrogel.

Figure 3. Chondrogenic differentiation of BMSCs in MI-hydrogel under an applied pressure. a) Schematic representation of the mechanical stimulation on BMSCs in MI-hydrogel. The MI-hydrogel is compressed via an indenter, exerting mechano-iontronic effects on the underlying GelMA embedded with cells. b) Confocal 3D reconstruction images of immunofluorescence staining, overlay images, and semi-quantitative fluorescence intensity analysis of BMSCs treated with compressed and non-compressed hydrogels, after 7 days of chondrogenic induction (n = 3). The fluorescence signals indicate the expression levels of chondrogenesis-related proteins SOX9 and COL2A1, as well as the piezoelectric-related protein Piezo1. Magnified views are provided below each image. Red, protein of interest; blue, nucleus. Scale bars, 100 µm for the full images and 200 µm for the magnified views. c–e) mRNA expression levels of SOX9, COL2A1, and Piezo1 in BMSCs encapsulated in GelMA under different treatments (n = 3). In (b), the experiments were independently repeated three times with similar results, and a representative result is shown for each. Data in (c) are presented as the mean ± SD. Statistical significance was determined using one-way ANOVA (multiple comparisons) followed by Tukey's post-hoc test. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001.

Figure 4. Promoted cartilage regeneration in vivo with MI-hydrogel implantation. a) Schematic representation and timeline of the experimentation on rats. Defects were created in the femoral knee joints of rats and implanted with I+ and I− hydrogels. While the rats remained stationary, almost no ionic polarization occurred. However, during exercise, compression of the hydrogel facilitated ion transport, ultimately promoting cartilage regeneration. b,f) Representative images of the gross view, H&E staining, SOFG staining, and immunofluorescence staining for the cartilage repair marker Col2a1 and the piezoelectric-related protein Piezo1 around the defect area at 4 or 8 weeks after rest for 4 weeks post-surgery. Black and white lines indicate the upper surface of the osteochondral area. c,d,g,h) Quantitative analysis of bone mineral density (BMD) and bone volume per tissue volume (BV/TV) in the subchondral bone remodeling area (n=3). e,i) Quantification of the healing extent in the cartilage defect area. In (b,f) the experiments were independently repeated three times with similar results, and a representative result is shown for each. Data in (c–e) and (g–i) are presented as the mean ± SD. Statistical significance was assessed using one-way ANOVA with multiple comparisons, followed by Tukey's post-hoc test. *P<0.05, **P<0.01, ***P<0.001, ****P<0.0001.

Figure 5. Overview of metabolic profile analyses of MI-hydrogel in cartilage. a) Schematic representation of the experimentation on cartilage of rats for metabolomic analysis. b) Statistical table of identified metabolites in cartilage of I+ M+, I− M+, I+ M−, and I− M− groups. c) A circular diagram showed the composition of the metabolites of this study. d–f) Clustering heat map of DEMs on d) I+ M+ group versus I− M+ group on week 4, e) I+ M+ group versus I− M− group on week 4, f) I+ M+ group versus I− M− group on week 4, revealing that massive DEMs were produced along with ionic-mechanical-coupled heterogeneous biological process. g–i) Venn diagram showed the relationship between different metabolites in g) I+ M+ group versus I− M+ group on week 4 and 8, h) I+ M+ group versus I− M− group on week 4 and 8, i) I+ M+ group versus I− M− group on week 4 and 8. j–l) Correlation of metabolic proximities showed the complex and tightly interaction signaling networks of metabolite categories in j) I+ M+ group versus I− M+ group on week 4, k) I+ M+ group versus I− M− group on week 4, l) I+ M+ group versus I− M− group on week 4.

Figure 6. Promoted cartilage regeneration via glutamine metabolism. a–d) Heatmap and volcano plots of DEGs showing that key metabolites in the main metabolic pathways in (a,c) I+ M+ group versus I− M− group on week 4, b,d) I+ M+ group versus I− M− group on week 8. e,f) Metabolic Set Enrichment Analysis (MSEA) of e) I+ M+ group versus I− M− group on week 4, f) I+ M+ group versus I− M− group on week 8, g–i) Correlation of metabolic proximities showed the complex and tightly interaction signaling networks of metabolite categories between the I+ M+ group versus the I− M− group on week 4, g) Correlation network plots of DEMs, h) Chord diagram of DEMs i) Spearman correlation plots. j) Bargraphs plot of representative DEGs in I+ M+, I− M+, I− M−, and I− M− groups on week 4. k) Scheme demonstration of metabolic reprogramming induced by exercise-reinforced ionic effect. Data in (j) are presented as the mean ± SD. Statistical significance was assessed using one-way ANOVA with multiple comparisons, followed by Tukey's post-hoc test.  $ ^{*}P<0.05 $,  $ ^{**}P<0.01 $,  $ ^{***}P<0.001 $,  $ ^{****}P<0.0001 $.

anchors.text: Figure 1 A self-powered RMI-ES system, based on BaTiO_{3}/PDMS piezoelectric composite films, was used to promote skin wound healing. It enhanced fibroblast proliferation, reduced inflammation, and promoted collagen deposition and new blood vessel formation through the PI3K/AKT pathway.

Figure 4(d) demonstrates the changes in output voltage under different frequencies of mechanical stimulation for the simple PDMS film and the PDMS-BTO composite film. The output voltage for both the simple PDMS film and the unpolarized PDMS-BTO composite film remains unchanged under pressure, generating only triboelectricity. The output of polarized PDMS-BTO composite film is observed to be 9 V at 1 Hz, 12.5 V at 2 Hz, and 16 V at 5 Hz. The pressure application is controlled by an external mechanical stimulation instrument, while the release is governed by the elasticity of the PDMS itself. Consequently, the release likely corresponds to slower processes, resulting in a smaller yet wider electrical signal [31].

anchors.text: FIGURE 1 Schematic of the articular cartilage. Different layers of articular cartilage from surface to depth include superficial, transitional, deep and calcified zones. The superficial zone consists of flattened ellipsoid chondrocytes oriented parallel to the joint surface. This area consists of collagen fibers with a high concentration, which are aligned parallel to the articular surface, proteoglycan content is low and contains the highest amount of water. The transitional zone is the thickest layer of cartilage that follows the superficial zone and is characterized by random collagen fibers. Chondrocytes in this area have a round shape and the concentration of proteoglycans is relatively higher than the superficial zone. In the deep zone, type II collagen fibers are oriented perpendicular to the joint surface and extend beyond the tidemark, which marks the border between the third and fourth zones. The deep zone contains collagen fibers with the largest diameter, the highest concentration of proteoglycan, and the lowest amount of water. The calcified zone forms a thin intermediate layer between the hyaline articular cartilage and the underlying subchondral bone. Chondrocytes in this region usually express a hypertrophic phenotype. (Created with BioRender.com).

FIGURE 2 The schematic diagram of the main three methods for the synthesis of the magnetic hydrogels. (A) The blending method. (B) The in situ precipitation method. (C) The grafting-onto method (Created with BioRender.com).

Figure 1a and Figure S2 (Supporting Information) show the fabrication process for the coiled PDA/CNT yarn (CPCY) that is the stretchable energy harvesting electrode in the CM-twistron harvester (Scheme 1b). A vertically-grown CNT forest was synthesized on a silicon wafer by using chemical vapor deposition (Figure S2a(i), Supporting Information).[29,30] Two CNT sheet layers were horizontally drawn from a side wall of this forest (Figure S2a(ii), Supporting Information), stacked together so they shared the same CNT alignment direction, and then twist inserted under mechanical load while one sheet-stack end was not torsionally tethered (Figure S2a(iii), Supporting Information). The non-tethering enables preparation of CNT yarn that has low density since it contains little yarn twist (Figure S2a(iv), Supporting Information).[26] This low-density CNT yarn was then immersed in a solution of dopamine and tris-HCl buffer to self-polymerize the dopamine while the PDA was inserted into the CNT yarn (Figure 1a). Figure 1b provides spectroscopic evidence that self-polymerization dopamine has been incorporated into the CNT yarn. The peaks at 1615, 1327, and 1028 cm $ ^{-1} $ correspond to catechol aromatic rings, methylene groups, and C–N stretching vibrations, respectively.[31–33] These functional groups within the PDA confer hydrophilicity to the CNT yarn in the cell growth medium, as shown in Figure 1b inset. The intrinsic contact angle measured on a flat PDA coated surface was 21.1° and 16.3° for advancing and receding angle, respectively. Due to the hydrophilicity of PDA and the porous structure of a CNT yarn, water wicks into the hydrophilic porous matrix resulting in fully wetting surface with 0° of water contact angle.[34] Scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) images of the cross-section of PDA-incorporated CNT yarn (PDA/CNT yarn) show that the PDA is evenly incorporated within the CNT yarn (Figure 1c). The incorporated PDA remains in the CNT yarn when the much further twist needed to generate a fully coiled CPCY is provided (Figures S2b and S3, Supporting Information).

anchors.text: Figure 1A. shows the FT-IR characteristic peaks of PVA and PVDF. For PVA, the peaks at 3337 cm $ ^{-1} $, 2943 cm $ ^{-1} $ and 1093 cm $ ^{-1} $ corresponded to the stretching vibration peak of -OH [18], the asymmetrical stretching vibration peak of -CH $ _2 $ and the stretching vibration peak of C-O, respectively. For pure PVDF, the peaks at 1402 cm $ ^{-1} $ and 1178 cm $ ^{-1} $ were attributed to the stretching vibration peaks of -CH $ _2 $ and C-F. The piezoelectric property of PVDF is mainly reflected in the characteristic peak of its piezoelectric  $ \beta $-phase at 840 cm $ ^{-1} $. For this reason, the FT-IR spectrum of PVA/PVDF composites was investigated, as shown in Figure 1B. The characteristic peaks of  $ \alpha $-phase,  $ \gamma $-phase and  $ \beta $-phase appeared at 976 cm $ ^{-1} $, 1234 cm $ ^{-1} $ and 840 cm $ ^{-1} $, respectively [19,20]. Compared with the spectra of pure PVA and pure PVDF, the characteristic peaks of PVA/PVDF composites showed no obvious shift or change. The results indicated that no chemical bonds were formed between PVA and PVDF, and the characteristic peak of the  $ \beta $-phase at 840 cm $ ^{-1} $ still existed; therefore, we inferred that the as-obtained composite materials should have the piezoelectric effect. In order to prove this conjecture, the piezoelectric property of the composites was tested, and the effects of PVA and PVDF content on the piezoelectric property were also investigated.

anchors.text: Fig. 1 Biogenesis, biomarkers, and cargos of exosomes. A Endocytosis and plasma membrane invagination enable extracellular constituents and cell surface proteins to invade cells. Early endosomes are formed when a plasmalemma buds and fuses with the endoplasmic reticulum, trans Golgi body, and mitochondrial constituents. Then, late endosomes are formed, which undergo a second invagination by cargo modification, resulting in the generation of various ILVs and the development of MVBs. The majority of MVBs will then be transferred to the plasmalemma and dock on the inner face, while others fuse with lysosomes via autophagosomes, causing their contents to be degraded. Finally, MVBs release ILVs to the outside of the cell through exocytosis and become exosomes. Exosomes originating from other cells may also be taken up by the cell in the meantime [28]. B Exosomes include a variety of nucleic acids, amino acids, proteins, and metabolites. Rab GTPases, ESCRT proteins (see text), and other proteins that are often recognized as exosome biomarkers are among the proteins implicated in exosome biogenesis (CD9, CD81, CD63, flotillin, TSG101, ceramide, and Alix). Proteins on the surface of exosomes include tetraspanins, integrins, and immunomodulatory proteins [26]. C Exosomes may also contain intracellular proteins, RNA, DNA, amino acids, and metabolites, among other things [34]. (Note: This figure was created by the authors and there is no conflict of copyright.)

Fig. 2 Macrophages can be induced to an activated inflammatory phenotype by exosomes secreted by MSCs/TSCs. Exosomes regulate the inflammation process after tendon injury to facilitate proper healing through M1 down-regulation and M2 up-regulation, which alleviate inflammation and determine whether repair or degeneration will occur [46–48]. (Note: This figure was created by the authors and there is no conflict of copyright.)

Exosomes also decrease the apoptosis of tenocytes. MMP and TIMP released by exosomes are the most important factors in aiding the healing process. TSCs-exos reduce MMP-3 and MMP-9 expression while increasing expression of metalloproteinase inhibitors (TIMP-1, TIMP-3) and improve tendons' mechanical properties. (Note: This figure was created by the authors and there is no conflict of copyright.)

anchors.text: Figure 1 | Electrical signals direct cell migration in wound healing and activate selected signalling pathways. a, Wounding induces lateral electric fields directed towards the wound centre (red arrow), by collapsing the local transepithelial potential difference (V). Black arrows represent sizes and directions of currents. b, Directly measured currents increase over time in rat corneal and human skin wounds. c, d, An electric field (EF) directs migration of corneal epithelial cells in a monolayer model of wound healing (150 mV mm $ ^{-1} $; c) and activates Akt (Ser 473), Src (Tyr 416), ERK and p38 in primary cultures of mouse keratinocyte and mouse peritoneal neutrophils in serum-free medium (200 mV mm $ ^{-1} $; d). Disrupting p110 $ \gamma $ attenuates activation of these signalling pathways. Phosphorylated JAK1 and JAK1 are shown as controls. e, Phosphorylated Src kinase polarizes in the direction of cell migration in electrotactic mouse keratinocytes (150 mV mm $ ^{-1} $). Scale bar, 20  $ \mu $m.

Figure 2 | Electrotaxis requires PI(3)Kγ. a–c, Impaired electrotactic responses in nonconfluent p110γ−/− keratinocytes. d–h, Attenuated electric field (EF)-directed migration of p110γ−/− keratinocytes in monolayer wound healing assays. Wild-type (p110γ+/+) cells are shown as controls. Electric fields that are applied with polarity opposite to the default healing direction direct the cells to move away from the wound (f, g). Red lines and blue arrows represent trajectories and direction of cell movement. Data (mean ± s.e.m.) were quantified from at least four independent experiments (c, h). *P < 0.05; **P < 0.01, Student’s t-test. Scale bars, 50 μm, EF = 200 mV mm−1. See also Supplementary Movies 7 (for a–c) and 8 (for d–h).

Figure 3 The tumour suppressor PTEN negatively regulates
electrotaxis. a, PTEN protein expression in keratinocytes. Four different
cultures for each genotype are shown. b, Loss of PTEN expression in
keratinocytes results in enhanced electric field (EF)-induced activation of
Akt and ERK. c, d, Increased electrostatic migration of nonconfluent
pten-deficient keratinocytes. e-g, Loss of PTEN increases migration of
keratinocytes in monolayer wound healing experiments in response to
electric fields directed into (e, g) or away from (f, g) the wound. Red lines
and blue arrows represent trajectories and direction of cell movement,
respectively. Data are representative of at least four independent
experiments with similar results. Quantification data are the mean ± s.e.m.
(d, g). Scale bars, 50 μm, EF = 200 mV mm⁻¹. *P < 0.05, Student’s t-test.
See also Supplementary Movies 12 (for c, d) and 13 (for e–g).

Figure 4 | PI(3)Kγ is required for electrostatic cell movement in wound healing of stratified epithelium in ex vivo cornea cultures. a, Stratified corneal epithelium migrate in situ to heal a wound (towards the left). b, This wound healing response is significantly enhanced by an electric field with the cathode at the wound. c, d, Impaired electric-field-mediated wound healing in corneas isolated from p110γ⁻/⁻ mice. e, Electric fields applied with polarity opposite to the default healing direction direct the wound edge to migrate away from the wound. f, This response is impaired when p110γ is disrupted. Results were confirmed in three or more independent experiments for each response. g, Quantification of the migration rates of the healing cornea epithelium from 3–7 experiments for a period of 120 min at each condition. Data are the mean ± s.e.m. EF = 150 mV mm⁻¹. Scale bars, 50 μm. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, Student’s t-test. See also Supplementary Movie 14.

anchors.text: Fig. 1. Normal cartilage of the distal femur in a young adult pig. (A) Gross specimen. The surface of the cartilage is dense white, glistening, and smooth. (B) Histology stained with safranin-O (original magnification, ×40). Matrix and chondrocytes are well organized in each zone. The superficial zone has no safranin-O staining. In the middle zone, where safranin-O staining appears, the cells are rounded or ovoid and seem to have random distribution; in contrast, in the deep zone, the cells are arranged in short columns.

Fig. 2. Transmission electron microscopy images of the distal femur in a normal rat. (A) Lamina splendens, the fine fibers and filaments in the surface of articular cartilage. (B) Elongated cells in the superficial zone. (C) A round cell in the deep zone. (Reprinted from Nakagawa Y, Muneta T, Otabe K, et al. Cartilage derived from bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells expresses lubricin in vitro and in vivo. PLoS One 2016;11(2):e014877; with permission.)

Col2 immunoreactive cartilage is shown in red; hCD146-expressing cells in green. Osteoclasts (oc), visualized by autofluorescence, resorb cartilage matrix and open up chondrocyte lacunae. G) Submacroscopic view of a pellet harvested at 40 days. An extensive portion of cartilage has been replaced by primitive stromal tissue (stroma). This is comprised between cortical bone and cartilage, is enriched in hematopoietic cells, and has a fully developed system of sinusoids. L,O) Cartilage is undergoing osteoclastic resorption (arrows), and osteoclasts penetrate through cartilage (arrows in O); resorption of cartilage is not coupled to deposition of new bone, but is associated with the appearance of stromal tissue (stroma).

anchors.text: Fig. 1. Schematic illustration of the fabrication process of graphene nanoplate (GNP)-carbon nanotube (CNT)-PDMS (GCP) ink and GCP composite. (a) Preparation process of GCP ink (b) Dip coating process of ear-cartilage-shaped PDMS substrate for ear-cartilage-shaped GCP composite collector and NGCP composite. (c) The printing process of GCP ink for stripe-patterned GCP composite collector and spatially controlled NGCP composite.

Fig. 3 addresses the surface characterization of the PDMS, the GCP-PDMS composite, and the NGCP-PDMS composite. Fig. 3a exhibits the image of the PDMS surface, and no particular morphology was observed from the surface image of PDMS. Fig. 3b shows the surface of the GCP-PDMS composite with the roughness formed by the carbon nanoparticles. Fig. 3c reveals the image of the nanofiber mat of the NGCP-PDMS composite. While the surface of the GCP-PDMS composite exhibited a certain level of roughness, we could obtain a flat electrospun nanofiber mat on the GCP-PDMS composite collector, which implied that the roughness of the GCP-PDMS composite would not significantly influence the electrospinning process. Fig. 3d shows the cross-section of the NGCP-PDMS composite where a thin layer of nanofiber mats was displayed on top of the GCP-PDMS composite. Furthermore, the inset of Fig. 3d revealed the fibrous structure of the nanofiber mat on the GCP-PDMS composite. Contact angle, which has known to influence cell adhesion when used in the biomedical field, was compared in Fig. 3e. PDMS and GCP-PDMS composite show high contact angles of about  $ 100^{\circ} $ due to the hydrophobicity of the PDMS. On the other hand, the NGCP composite shows a much lower contact angle of about  $ 30^{\circ} $ due to the hydrophilicity of the gelatin in electrospun nanofibers, which would result in better cell adhesion.

Fig. 3. SEM images of PDMS (a), GCP-PDMS composite (b), NGCP-PDMS composite (c), and cross-sectioned NGCP-PDMS composite (d). Inset of (d): the fibrous structure of the nanofiber mat in the NGCP-PDMS composite. Scale bars are 100 µm for (a, b, and d) and 10 µm for (c). (e) The water contact angle of PDMS, GCP-PDMS composite collector, and NGCP-PDMS composite.

Fig. 4. (a) Sheet resistance of PDMS and GCP composite collector with 3%, 5%, 10%, and 15% carbon nanoparticle concentration. (b) Electrospun nanofiber mats on PDMS and GCP composite collectors with 3%, 5%, 10%, and 15% carbon nanoparticle concentration, and Al. (c) The thickness of fibrous structures in nanofiber mats on the 3% and 5% GCP composite collectors. Scale bars are 10 μm. (d) Thickness comparison of nanofiber mats on each collector. (e) The sheet resistance of 5% carbon nanoparticle concentration with different thicknesses.

Fig. 5. The direction of the electric fields with the collector system (a-(i)), electric field simulations of PDMS (a-(ii)), 3% (a-(iii)) and 5% GCP composites, and metal collector (a-(iv)). (b) y-component of the electric field along the imaginary line above PDMS, 3% and 5% GCP composites, and metal collector. (c) Average y-component of the electric field along the imaginary line above each collector.

Fig. 6. (a) GCP composite collectors with different carbon nanoparticle concentrations. Scale bars are 1 cm. (b) SEM images of GCP composites. Scale bars are 10 μm. (c) The stress-strain curves with different carbon nanoparticle concentrations. (d) the stress-strain curves of 5% carbon nanoparticle concentration with different thicknesses of the GCP composite.

Fig. 7. Stress-strain curves (a) and Young's modulus (b) of pure PDMS and 5% GCP-PDMS with three different PDMS mixing ratios. Stress-strain curves (c) and Young's modulus (d) of pure PDMS, 5% GCP-PDMS, and 5% NGCP-PDMS with a PDMS mixing ratio of 10:1.

Fig. 8. (a) Ear-cartilage-shaped NGCP-PDMS composite. Scale bar is 1 cm. (b) Folding and unfolding procedures with ear-cartilage-shaped NGCP-PDMS composite. SEM images (c), the thickness (d), and the diameter population of nanofibers (e) of deposited nanofiber mats on different locations of the ear-cartilage-shaped NGCP-PDMS composite. Scale bars are 10 μm.

Fig. 9. (a) Live/dead assay images of PDMS, GCP-PDMS, NGCP-PDMS, and fibronectin-coated NGCP-PDMS composite. Scale bars are 250  $ \mu $m. (b) Cell proliferation of four samples: PDMS, GCP-PDMS, NGCP-PDMS, and fibronectin-coated NGCP-PDMS composite. (c) The in vivo implantation image of the ear-cartilage-shaped NGCP-PDMS composite in a rat model before and after 2 weeks. (d) H&E staining images of PDMS, GCP-PDMS, NGCP-PDMS, and fibronectin-coated NGCP-PDMS composite at 2 weeks after subcutaneous implantation in a rat model. Scale bars are 200  $ \mu $m.

Fig. 2a and b presents patterned GCP composite collectors produced by printing a GCP ink and spatially controlled nanofiber mats on the patterned GCP composite collectors. The patterned GCP composite collectors, represented in Fig. 2a–(i) and b–(i), were printed as a stripe pattern and a letter pattern of "PNU". Given that the GCP ink could be printed using a 3D printer, the pattern of the GCP composite collector can be readily controllable and possesses a high degree of freedom in the shape of the pattern. Subsequent electrospinning on the patterned GCP composite collectors produced patterned electrospun nanofiber mats (Fig. 2a–(ii) and b–(ii)). Furthermore, electrospinning on a stripe-patterned GCP composite collector produced not only a strip-patterned nanofiber mat on the GCP composite collector but also induced the alignment of electrospun nanofibers owing to the concentrated electric field (Fig. 2a–(ii)) [11]. Fig. 2a–(ii) shows the rolled-up formation of the patterned NGCP composite and SEM images of aligned nanofibers, and Fig. 2b–(ii) shows the deposited nanofiber mats on the letter-patterned GCP composite. Fig. 2c–(i) and c–(ii) show a 3D hollow cylindrical and bifurcated blood-vessel nanofiber scaffold, respectively. The utilization of the water-soluble PVA substrate and GCP composite collector facilitated the removal of the GCP composite collector after electrospinning, and achieved a 3D hollow bifurcated blood-vessel nanofiber scaffold, which could be difficult to be produced by a conventional electrospinning process. Given that both nanofiber scaffolds consisted of only electrospun nanofibers without any support, the 3D hollow bifurcated blood-vessel nanofiber scaffold demonstrated self-standing ability. Fig. 2d and e exhibited 3D GCP-PDMS composite collectors and corresponding 3D NGCP-PDMS composites. Fig. 2d–(i) and e–(i) represent ear-cartilage-shaped and knee-cartilage-shaped GCP-PDMS composite collectors. We confirmed that the GCP composite entirely covered the 3D PDMS substrate, demonstrating the effectiveness of the dip coating method for coating a GCP ink on a 3D complicated-shaped substrate. Fig. 2d–(ii) and e–(ii) show 3D NGCP composites fabricated by electrospinning on a 3D GCP composite collector. By utilizing conformal electrospinning with flattening of the 3D GCP composite collector, the electrospun nanofiber mats were uniformly deposited. The diameter distribution of deposited nanofibers on GCP composite collectors was presented in Fig. 2f. Given that most of the electrospun nanofiber on the GCP composite have nanoscale thickness, we concluded that the GCP composite is an effective collector for electrospinning to produce electrospun nanofibers.

Fig. 2 In vitro evaluation of the biocompatibility and collagen synthesis ability of fibrin glue showed that fibrin glue did not influence the viability and enduring proliferation but enhanced the collagen synthesis ability of tendon stem/progenitor cells. (A) Live/dead staining was performed on tendon stem/progenitor cells encapsulated in fibrin glue and cocultured for 1, 4, and 7 days. Calcein AM was used for live cells (green) and propidium iodide for dead cells (red). Scale bar: 100 μm. (B) Quantitative analysis of the viability of tendon stem/progenitor cells encapsulated in fibrin glue and cocultured for 1, 4, and 7 days. (C) CCK-8 cell proliferation assay of tendon stem/progenitor cells cultured with leach liquor of fibrin glue compared with those cultured with growth medium for 1, 4, and 7 days. (D) Sirius red staining of tendon stem/progenitor cells cultured with or without fibrin glue coating. Scale bar: 200 μm. (E) Quantitative analysis of Sirius red staining for tendon stem/progenitor cells cultured with or without fibrin glue coating showed that fibrin glue enhanced the collagen synthesis ability of tendon stem/progenitor cells; OD = optical density.

Fig. 3 The cell growth and collagen deposition of tissue-engineered bicipital tendon patches showed ongoing proliferation of cells, resulting in abundant collagen Type I construction. (A) Live cell staining demonstrates cell growth from tissue-engineered bicipital tendon patches cultured for 1, 7, 11, and 14 days. Calcein AM was used for live cells (green). Scale bar: 200 μm. (B) Quantitative analysis of cell growth area of tissue-engineered bicipital tendon patch cultured for 1, 7, 11, and 14 days. (C) H&E staining (original magnification, 20X) and (D) immunohistochemical staining of collagen Type I (original magnification, 20X) of sections of tissue-engineered bicipital tendon patches cultured for 21 and 28 days. Scale bar: 100 μm.

Fig. 4 Macroscopic and histological evaluation of regenerated tendon at 1 month in vivo. (A) This schematic illustration shows the surgical procedure for tissue-engineered bicipital autologous tendon patch transplantation. (B) The macroscopic view of regenerated tendon in the control, gel, and patch groups indicated better repair effect in the patch group, which closely resembles the surrounding uninjured tendon in morphology, with a blurred boundary between the repaired tissue and the surrounding normal tendon. (C) Representative H&E staining (original magnification, 10X), polarized light (original magnification, 10X), and Masson trichrome staining (original magnification, 30X) were conducted to evaluate the repair outcomes of the control group, gel group, and patch group. The findings demonstrated that the patch group showed noticeable signs of tendon regeneration and the presence of partially organized and mature collagen synthesis, in contrast to the control and gel groups. Scale bar: 200 μm or 50 μm.

Fig. 5 (A) The total histological scoring and (B) histological scoring of six separate parameters of regenerated tendon at 1 month in the control group, gel group, and patch group demonstrated the lowest scores in the patch group, revealing better repair of the patch group compared with both the control and gel groups.

Fig. 6 (A) This image shows transmission electron microscopy analysis of the regenerated tendon tissues at 1 month. Longitudinal and transverse cross-sections of collagen fibrils showed that the collagen fibrils in the patch group exhibited the most compact and orderly bundle-like structure, surpassing those observed in the gel group and control group. Scale bar: 1 μm or 0.2 μm. (B) The quantitative analysis results demonstrated that the patch group and gel group exhibited larger average diameter of regenerated collagen fibrils compared with the control group. The distribution ranges of the collagen fibril diameters in (C) the control group, (D) gel group, and (E) patch group are shown here. (F) The quantitative analysis of the angle distribution of collagen fibrils orientation demonstrated that the distribution of regenerated collagen fibrils in the patch group was more regular and orderly compared with both the gel group and control group. A color image accompanies the online version of this article.

Fig. 7 Macroscopic and histological evaluation of tendon regeneration at 3 months in vivo. (A) The macroscopic view of regenerated tendon in the control, gel, and patch groups indicated better repair effect in the patch group, which closely resembles the surrounding normal tendon. Quantitative analysis of infraspinatus tendon width of (B) the control group (blue), (C) gel group (green), and (D) patch group (red). (E) Representative H&E staining (original magnification, 10X), polarized light (original magnification, 10X), and Masson trichrome staining (original magnification, 30X) were conducted to evaluate the repair outcomes of the control, gel, and patch groups. The findings demonstrated that the patch group showed evident signs of tendon regeneration and the presence of organized and mature collagen synthesis, in contrast to the control and gel groups. Scale bar: 200 μm or 50 μm.

Fig. 8 (A) The total histological scoring and (B) histological scoring of six separate parameters of regenerated tendon at 3 months in the control, gel, and patch groups demonstrated the lowest scores in the patch group, revealing better repair of the patch group compared with both the control and gel groups.

Fig. 9 (A) This image shows TEM analysis of the regenerated tendon tissues at 3 months. Longitudinal and transverse cross-sections of collagen fibrils showed that the collagen fibrils in the patch group exhibited the most compact and orderly bundle-like structure, surpassing those observed in the gel and control groups. Scale bar: 1 μm or 0.2 μm. (B) The quantitative analysis results demonstrated that the patch group exhibited larger average diameter of regenerated collagen fibril compared with the control and gel groups. The distribution ranges of the collagen fibril diameters in (C) the control group, (D) gel group, and (E) patch group are shown here. (F) The quantitative analysis of the angle distribution of collagen fibril orientations demonstrated that the distribution of regenerated collagen fibrils in the patch group was more regular and orderly compared with both the gel and control groups. A color image accompanies the online version of this article.

Fig. 10 Transcriptional analysis of regenerated tendons from 1 month to 3 months. (A) In the repair process of the patch group and gel group at different points (1, 2, and 3 months) after transplantation, differential gene expression trajectory clustering revealed that the patch group exhibited lower levels of immune and inflammatory response (Cluster 1), higher levels of protein transport and collagen synthesis (Cluster 6), and lower inclination toward ossification (Cluster 8). In the hot maps and bubble plots, the colors represent the magnitude of gene expression, with red indicating high expression and blue indicating low expression. Additionally, in the bubble plots, the bubble size represents the number of differentially expressed genes associated with the term, with larger dots indicating a greater number of genes. (B) Enrichment maps of differential pathways across tendon repair between the patch group and gel group were found in an integrative analysis by the p value of differential analysis; these pathways included those related to chemotaxis, anatomical structure morphogenesis, and cell-related pathways. The colors represent different time points. Multicolored nodes indicate pathways that were enriched according to several time points of evidence. Each node represents an enriched Gene Ontology (GO) term, with node size corresponding to the number of differentially expressed genes enriched in that GO term. (C) The difference between both groups at 1 month and 3 months by GSEA is shown here. Stem cell proliferation and cell adhesion were enriched in the patch group at 1 month (red), and collagen-related pathways were enriched in the patch group at 3 months (blue); NES = normalized enrichment score.

anchors.text: Fig. 1 High concentrations of copper inhibit the growth of S. aureus. Wild type S. aureus SH1000 were inoculated to a starting OD₅₉₅nm of 0.03 into (A) two types of rich media, tryptic soy broth (TSB – black bars) or LB (grey bars), or (B) two types of minimal media, glucose-containing chemically defined medium (CDM – black bars) or Tris-minimal (TM) medium lacking glucose (grey bars), each supplemented with increasing concentrations of CuSO₄. The cultures were incubated for 5 h at 37 °C with orbital shaking (180 rpm), and the final OD₅₉₅nm values were recorded. Growth is inhibited by high levels of copper in all media, but this toxicity effect is greatest in the minimal media. The symbols represent statistical significance based on a Student’s t-test, where ns = not significant,  $ * = p < 0.05 $,  $ ** = p < 0.005 $, and  $ *** = p < 0.0005 $.

Fig. 2 S. aureus cells accumulate additional copper when cultured in high concentrations of copper. Wild type S. aureus SH1000 were inoculated to a starting OD₅₉₅nm of 0.05 into TM media (containing glucose) either with (Cu-treated) or without (control) the addition of 1 mM CuSO₄, and incubated for 6 h at 37 °C with 180 rpm orbital shaking. Cell densities were determined by OD₅₉₅nm, and equal cell numbers were harvested, washed to remove surface-bound metals, digested in concentrated HNO₃, and elemental composition of the resulting acid lysates was determined by ICP-MS. The symbols represent statistical significance, based on a Student’s t-test, where  $ *** = p < 0.0005 $.

Fig. 3 Metal distribution in S. aureus cytosolic extracts. Cytosolic extracts were prepared from S. aureus SH1000 cells, cultured in TSB medium either (A) without or (B) with addition of 500 μM CuSO₄. Extracts were resolved by anion exchange chromatography (1 mL HiTrap Q HP column) in 20 mM Hepes, pH 8.0, and eluted with stepwise increases in NaCl concentration. Resulting fractions were subjected to a second dimension of separation by HPLC size exclusion chromatography (SW3000 column) in 5 mM Hepes, 50 mM NaCl, pH 7.5. Elemental composition of the resulting fractions were determined by ICP-MS, shown by the height of the peaks on the z-axis. Accumulation of copper in one major pool was observed in cells cultured in excess copper, whereas the accumulation of zinc was decreased in high molecular weight pools. Manganese accumulation was unchanged. All lysate preparation and chromatography steps were performed under anaerobic conditions.

Fig. 4 Purification of copper-associated GapA from extracts of copper-exposed S. aureus cells. S. aureus SH1000 cells (biomass from a total of 2.5 L culture) were cultured in TSB medium containing 50 μM CuSO₄, harvested and washed as described (see Methods). Cell extract was prepared and resolved by liquid chromatography under anaerobic conditions. The soluble cell fraction was initially passed through a hydroxyapatite column in 5 mM sodium phosphate, pH 6.8 (data not shown), and then the unbound flow-through fraction was buffered by an on-conditioned cell method (see methods). The flow-through was subsequently resolved by an on-conditioned cell method (see methods). The cell fraction was then removed from the cell-based gel (black) and the protein content (black triangles) and for copper (blue circles) by ICP-MS. (B) An aliquot (500 μL) of the peak copper-containing fraction from AEC was subsequently resolved by SEC on a Superdex 200 Increase column in 20 mM Tris, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, analysed for protein by A280nm (black) and for copper by ICP-MS (blue). (C) Fractions around the copper peak were analysed by SDS-PAGE, and the protein band identified by peptide mass fingerprinting as GapA is indicated by an arrow. (D) Selected fractions were also assayed for GAPDH activity (red squares), which co-migrated with the copper.

Fig. 5 The GapA-associated copper pool is absent in the  $ \Delta $gapA mutant strain. The S. aureus SH1000 wild type and the  $ \Delta $gapA mutant strain were cultured in TM medium (0.5 L) with no added glucose but containing 50  $ \mu $M  $ CuSO_4 $. Extracts were prepared and resolved under anaerobic conditions by AEC, and the fraction eluted by 400 mM NaCl from the wild type extract was found to contain most of the GAPDH activity. Aliquots (500  $ \mu $L) of the 400 mM NaCl AEC fractions from each strain were further resolved by SEC on a Superdex 200 Increase column in 10 mM Tris, 150 mM NaCl, pH 7.5. SEC fractions were analysed for copper (blue circles: closed = WT, open =  $ \Delta $gapA mutant) by ICP-MS and for GAPDH activity using an enzyme assay (black triangles) (A). Note that the SEC fractions from the  $ \Delta $gapA mutant strain were devoid of GAPDH activity (data not shown). SDS-PAGE analysis of selected SEC fractions from both the wild type (B) and the  $ \Delta $gapA mutant (C) confirmed that the protein distribution was essentially unchanged between the two chromatographs, with the exception of the presence of the  $ \sim $36 kDa GapA band (highlighted by a red asterisk) in the wild type fractions that was absent in the  $ \Delta $gapA mutant samples (also indicated with a red asterisk).

Fig. 6 S. aureus cells cultured in the presence of copper exhibit reduced GAPDH activity. S. aureus SH1000 cells were cultured in TSB medium in the absence (control sample – 1, black) or presence (high [Cu] sample – 2, dark blue) of 0.5 mM CuSO₄. The cells were washed extensively in EDTA, and then lysed in the absence of EDTA, and the extracts assayed for GAPDH activity, demonstrating a reduction in enzymatic activity in cells cultured in the presence of elevated copper. The lysate that was prepared from cells cultured in the presence of copper was subsequently treated in vitro with a copper chelator, through anaerobic incubation of the extract for 10 min in the presence of 100 μM BCS (light blue), which resulted in increased GAPDH activity, implying Cu(I) chelation had alleviated GAPDH inhibition. Likewise, anaerobic incubation of the control lysate with 10 μM Cu(I) (dark grey) reduced the activity, which was reversed on subsequent addition of BCS (light grey).
